significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would license the conclusion that multilingual LLMs contain a compact cross-language negation operator whose causal steering flips polarity, while negative-concord and multiple-marker typologies predict greater scope and double-negation errors through disruption of that operator. This combines a form-(ii) causal mechanism—"steering along the shared negation direction can causally flip" and repair errors—with a form-(iii) ordering between independently identifiable negation typologies and error rates, fixing expectations across languages rather than merely establishing that negation is represented. The phenomenon and mechanism are both determinate enough that componentwise negative results would rule out either cross-language sharing, typology-graded interference, or causal repair, although failure of the bundled hypothesis as a whole would be less informative without identifying the failed component; Shaitarova and Rinaldi's 2021 cross-lingual negation-scope work confirms that typology-linked transfer is a substantive explanatory question. Topic substitution fails: deleting the specific negation operator, negative-concord disruption, and typology-error ordering leaves only the generic shared-versus-language-specific topic, which would not warrant this score.

reach.justification: The principal handle is the claimed "shared negation direction," an inference-time intervention that can "flip polarity" and "repair negation-typology-induced errors"; the typology-to-error relationship also supplies a diagnostic for language classes at elevated risk. The steering handle is ex ante with respect to the model's final interpretation because it acts inside the forward pass, while activation localization and error scoring are primarily post hoc. Although the direction would require re-extraction per model, the substantive conclusion predicts what recalibration should recover—cross-language sharing plus greater disruption for negative-concord or multiple-marker constructions—so more than a search procedure transfers across the asserted class of multilingual LLMs; likely downstream users include multilingual-model auditors and developers deploying models on negation-sensitive tasks. Topic substitution fails here as well: the broad multilingual-representation topic alone supplies neither this named intervention nor the transferable typology-risk ordering.
